title: Google speeds protein structure prediction 8.6-fold to advance targeted cancer research
key_facts: Google researchers developed a method that speeds protein structure prediction by 8.6 times, per Google, without sacrificing structural accuracy in its tests.
The method, "surgical epitope excision", focuses predictions on the local region where a designed protein is expected to attach.
It was applied to design proteins binding fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP), a molecule associated with solid tumours.
The strongest lab-tested designs reached single-digit nanomolar binding affinity.
In a computational comparison with equal computing, a scientist working with an agent got nearly twice the predicted hit rate of a scientist alone.
Two other Google projects: DNA aptamers reached 33.5% (myoglobin) and 42.1% (alpha-thrombin) confirmed on-target hit rates by round three, and VERID, a digital lab model for robotic experiments.
The systems are experimental and the binders have not been shown to work as cancer treatments.
quote_evidence: According to Google, the approach accelerated structure prediction by 8.6 times without sacrificing structural accuracy in its tests.
The strongest experimentally tested designs achieved single-digit nanomolar binding affinity, indicating a tight molecular interaction.
However, the systems remain experimental, and the protein binders have not been demonstrated as cancer treatments.
why_it_matters_hint: Cheaper protein design could shorten early drug discovery, but nothing is shown to treat cancer yet.
event_date: Reported 16 Oct 2026 (Google release date not stated)
notes: Company's own results as relayed by Interesting Engineering; no outside review reported.
